newsitem.title: UK: UK's FTSE seen falling short-term as rates turn.
newsitem.headline: UK's FTSE seen falling short-term as rates turn.

text.p: The UK's FTSE 100 index is likely to extend its current decline in the short term as rate fears grip markets on both sides of the Atlantic, strategists said on Thursday.
A drop on Wall Street sent the UK blue chip index sharply lower in afternoon trading after Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan signalled tighter credit at next week's monetary policy meeting.
Investors would be watching for the size of next week's U.S. rate hike and any indication of future policy moves, though a pre-emptive move now could avert stronger medicine later in the year.
By 1559 GMT the FTSE 100 was down 71.4 points at 4,260.8, after earlier dropping to a seven-week low of 4,251.5.
"This is what we have been expecting for some time," said Andy Hartwill, strategist at SocGen.
"4,150 is our near-term target for the FTSE 100. The proximate cause is the possibility of an interest rate hike which is exposing high stock market valuations in the UK and United States."
"But I would be happy to buy the market not far below its current level," Hartwill said,

"In the end the cycle is likely to be different from previous cycles, the degree of monetary tightening is going to be less and the opportunity for a pre-emptive move will probably moderate the scale of the rate cycle."
"If we get 75 or 100 basis points over the next 12 months, in the end that is not a significant tightening, but the risks short term are on the downside," Hartwill said.
Other pundits also saw shares coming under further pressure in the short term.
"Mentally and technically the market is tired," said Kirit Shah, strategist at Sanwa International.
"If the Fed tightens interest rates next week and the Dow falls, 4,100 (on FTSE 100) is pretty much on the cards, and possibly 4,000."
Shah noted that most market participants believe UK interest rates will also be bumped up following the British general election on May 1.
"The FTSE will be a bit better protected than the Dow on the downside, but in the UK we are also likely to face rate hikes," he said.
"In the medium-term the FTSE could outperform the Dow, but it would probably be better to just stay away for now."
Scott Evans, strategist at UBS, said a correction in markets had been expected after sharp gains in leading indices across Europe in the early weeks of the year.
Evans pointed out that worries over progress towards monetary union were also dragging down European markets.
"All our year-end targets for the FTSE and European indexes were passed about a month ago and it could be a little while before markets start to claw their way back," Evans said.
"What we need to wait for is some more certainty on EMU and the extent of any rise in (U.S.) rates...Short term the outlook is grim but longer term it is probably OK."
